title: Modern natural law: Finnis
subtitle: Practical reasonableness, the seven basic goods, and determinatio
objectives: Explain how Finnis reconstructs natural law as a theory of practical reasonableness, without relying on theology or a claimed inference from facts to values
List and briefly explain Finnis's seven basic goods, and explain why he treats them as self-evident rather than derived
Explain determinatio — how positive law 'determines' (specifies) the requirements of natural law through reasonable choice, without being strictly deduced from it

leadingAuthorities.citation: Finnis, Natural Law and Natural Rights (1980)
leadingAuthorities.role: The leading modern restatement of natural law as a theory of practical reasonableness, built on the seven basic goods and determinatio

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Finnis is the natural law theory most likely to appear against Hart directly in an exam, precisely because he doesn't rely on theology and so can't be dismissed as a religious position. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You can list the seven goods — this lesson checks whether you can use determinatio to explain why a specific speed limit can be both a free human choice and, once made, binding.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans on determinatio: expect scenarios asking whether a rule specifies natural law or is simply deduced from it.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — Finnis's break from Aquinas's theological framing, and his insistence the basic goods are self-evident rather than inferred, are easy to blur together if you rush.

overview.hook: Why does it matter, morally, which side of the road you drive on? It doesn't — and yet once a jurisdiction picks a side, driving on the other one becomes genuinely, seriously wrong, not just illegal on a technicality. John Finnis built an entire modern revival of natural law around exactly this puzzle: how a free, reasonable, non-inevitable human choice can become something you are bound to follow. This lesson is his answer, and it owes almost nothing to theology.

parts.heading: Natural law without the theology
parts.voice: argumentative — states what Finnis keeps and what he drops from the previous lesson
body: The previous lesson's Aquinas is built on a theological scaffold: eternal law as God's plan, natural law as participation in it, human law as a further derivation. Finnis, writing in 1980, wants to defend a recognisably natural law position — that law is answerable to a rational moral order beyond mere enactment — without asking a reader to first accept that scaffold.

His route in is practical reason, not metaphysics. Finnis starts from a straightforward observation: human beings reason about what to do, and some of what they reason towards is intelligibly, self-evidently good — worth pursuing for its own sake, not merely as a means to something else. A theory of natural law, on his account, is really a theory of practical reasonableness: an account of the basic forms of human flourishing that give anyone a reason to act, and the requirements of reasonableness that structure how those reasons should be weighed against each other.

This matters for how you should present Finnis in an exam. He is not simply 'Aquinas without God' — dropping theology changes what has to do the justificatory work, and Finnis is explicit that his account does not depend on, and is not an argument for, theism, even though he personally goes on (in the book's final chapters) to connect his theory to a further, separate argument about God. The seven basic goods, and the derivation of positive law from them, are meant to stand on their own.

components.definition: Finnis's central organising idea: the capacity to reason about what to do, grasping certain basic forms of human flourishing as self-evidently worth pursuing, and structuring action in accordance with requirements (such as impartiality between persons and coherence between one's commitments) that mark reasoning as genuinely reasonable rather than merely self-interested.

interaction.prompt: Is Finnis's Natural Law and Natural Rights best described as 'Aquinas's theory restated with the theology removed and nothing else changed'?
options: No — dropping the theological scaffold changes what does the justificatory work, and Finnis builds his own independent case from practical reason and self-evident basic goods
Yes — Finnis simply deletes the references to God from Aquinas's argument and leaves the rest intact
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Finnis reconstructs the justification from the ground up using practical reasonableness and self-evident basic goods, rather than lifting Aquinas's argument and deleting the theological premises.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — removing theology isn't a cosmetic edit to Aquinas's argument. Finnis has to supply an entirely independent justificatory foundation, which is what practical reasonableness and the basic goods are for.

parts.heading: The seven basic goods
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Finnis identifies seven basic forms of human good — self-evidently worthwhile ends that give anyone, in any culture, a reason for action. They are not ranked in order of importance, and none is meant to be reducible to, or a means towards, any of the others; each is an independent, irreducible value.

The seven are: life (including bodily health and the transmission of life through procreation); knowledge (the pursuit of truth for its own sake, distinct from merely useful information); play (activity engaged in for its own enjoyment, with no further purpose required); aesthetic experience (the appreciation of beauty, whether or not one also produces it); sociability, or friendship (acting for the sake of another's wellbeing and one's own, in a relationship of mutual regard); practical reasonableness itself (the good of bringing one's own intelligence to bear on one's own choices and character, using freedom well); and religion, in a broad sense (the good of situating oneself correctly in relation to the ultimate order of things, however that is understood — not necessarily a commitment to any particular faith).

Two features of this list matter for how it's used later in the lesson. First, Finnis insists these goods are self-evident, not derived: you cannot argue someone into recognising knowledge as worth pursuing for its own sake the way you can argue them into a conclusion from premises — you can only get them to see it, typically by pointing out that even someone who denies knowledge is valuable is, in denying it, engaged in exactly the kind of inquiry the denial dismisses. Second, because the goods are irreducible and unranked, practical life constantly requires reasonably weighing commitments to several of them at once — which is exactly the job the 'requirements of practical reasonableness' (a further, more detailed part of Finnis's theory beyond this lesson's scope) are meant to do.

components.label: Finnis's seven basic goods
points: Life — including bodily health and the transmission of life
Knowledge — the pursuit of truth for its own sake
Play — activity valuable for its own enjoyment
Sociability (friendship) — acting for another's wellbeing in a relationship of mutual regard
Practical reasonableness — bringing one's own intelligence to bear on one's own choices and character
Religion (broadly) — situating oneself correctly in relation to the ultimate order of things

interaction.prompt: This isn't a ranking exercise — Finnis insists the seven goods are unranked — but for recall, place these four goods in the order this lesson lists them.
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Correct order for recall purposes — though remember the substantive point: Finnis treats all seven goods as unranked and irreducible to one another, so this sequence is a memory aid, not a hierarchy.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the lesson's list again — and regardless of the order you chose, remember the substantive point that Finnis does not rank these goods against each other at all.

parts.heading: Determinatio: specifying natural law without deducing from it
parts.voice: case-narrative — works through a concrete example before naming the doctrine
body: Return to the driving example from this lesson's hook. Nothing in natural law tells you whether traffic should keep to the left or the right — both options are equally consistent with the basic good of life (avoiding collisions) and practical reasonableness (coordinated, predictable behaviour). Yet once a jurisdiction chooses one, driving on the other side becomes seriously wrong, not merely against a rule you're free to weigh up for yourself.

Finnis revives Aquinas's term for this: determinatio, usually translated 'determination' in the sense of specification. A determinatio is not a logical deduction from natural law's requirements, the way a mathematical theorem is deduced from axioms — natural law radically underdetermines which side of the road to drive on. It is instead a reasonable choice, made by a properly authorised lawmaker, that settles one of several options natural law leaves genuinely open, in order to serve a good (here, coordinated safety) that natural law does require in the abstract.

This is the move that does the heaviest lifting in Finnis's account of positive law's authority. Because a determinatio serves a genuine requirement of practical reasonableness (coordination is itself required by practical reasonableness, even though no particular scheme of coordination is), the resulting rule inherits real binding force — you cannot escape it just by pointing out that the other side of the road would have worked equally well. The making of the choice, by an authority with standing to make it, is what completes the natural law's own unfinished requirement.

components.definition: A reasonable choice made by a properly authorised lawmaker that settles one of several options natural law leaves open, in order to serve a good that natural law requires only in the abstract — distinguished from a strict logical deduction, because natural law itself does not determine which specific option must be chosen.

interaction.prompt: Which of the following is a determinatio in Finnis's sense, rather than a straightforward deduction from natural law?
interaction.scenarioA: A legislature sets the speed limit on a specific residential road at 20mph, when 25mph or 15mph would have served road safety about equally well
interaction.scenarioB: A court concludes that a statute permitting the deliberate killing of a randomly selected innocent person for entertainment is invalid, because it directly negates the basic good of life
interaction.explanation: A is a determinatio: natural law requires road safety in the abstract, but leaves the exact figure genuinely open between several reasonable options, and the legislature's choice among them is what creates the specific binding rule. B is closer to a direct application (or, on Finnis's more careful account, a case falling outside the focal meaning of law altogether) — no real range of reasonable options exists once a rule directly negates a basic good.

parts.heading: Self-evidence, not the naturalistic fallacy
parts.voice: Socratic — poses the standard objection before showing Finnis's answer
body: The most common objection to any natural law theory is the naturalistic fallacy: the charge that you cannot validly derive an 'ought' (a value judgement) purely from an 'is' (a fact about human nature), because no amount of description of how things are logically entails a conclusion about how they should be.

Finnis's answer is not to bite the bullet and defend a fact-to-value inference. It is to deny that his theory makes one at all. He insists the basic goods are grasped as self-evident by practical understanding — not inferred from prior facts about human nature through a chain of reasoning that a sceptic could challenge premise by premise. On his account, you don't reason your way to 'knowledge is good' starting from biological or psychological facts about human beings; you simply grasp it, in much the same way you grasp basic logical or mathematical truths, once you understand what is being proposed and reflect on your own practical engagement with inquiry.

Critics remain unconvinced that this escapes the objection cleanly — some argue that calling something 'self-evident' is doing exactly the derivation-work Hume's fork rules out, just relabelled; others accept Finnis's method for some goods but doubt it can secure exactly seven, no more and no fewer. You are not required to resolve that dispute. What you are required to do is state precisely what Finnis claims — a self-evidence thesis, not a fact-to-value inference — before you go on to evaluate whether that claim succeeds.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often write that Finnis 'derives' the basic goods from facts about human nature, and then criticise him for committing the naturalistic fallacy as if he had conceded the inference.
components.whyItsWrong: Finnis explicitly denies making any such derivation. His claim is that the basic goods are self-evident to practical understanding, not inferred from prior factual premises about human nature. A fair critique has to engage with the self-evidence claim on its own terms — for instance, disputing that all seven goods really are self-evident, or that 'self-evidence' avoids doing the same work an is-ought inference would — rather than accusing Finnis of a move he explicitly disclaims making.

interaction.prompt: Tap the phrase in this student answer that misstates Finnis's actual position on the naturalistic fallacy.
interaction.scenarioText: Finnis argues that the seven basic goods are self-evident to practical reason, and he derives this self-evidence from prior biological facts about what human beings need to survive, which is exactly the is-ought inference Hume warned against.
tappableSpans: the seven basic goods are self-evident to practical reason
derives this self-evidence from prior biological facts
the is-ought inference Hume warned against
interaction.correctSpan: derives this self-evidence from prior biological facts
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Finnis explicitly denies deriving the basic goods from prior biological or factual premises — his claim is that they are grasped as self-evident by practical understanding, not inferred through a chain of reasoning from facts about human nature.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: The first phrase accurately states Finnis's self-evidence claim, and the reference to Hume's fork is a fair description of the standard objection. The error is the middle clause, which wrongly attributes to Finnis a derivation from biological facts that he explicitly disclaims making.

parts.heading: Legal validity, revisited: Finnis's focal meaning
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by comparing Finnis back to Aquinas
body: One more refinement separates Finnis from the previous lesson's Aquinas, and it is worth being precise about it. Aquinas's lex injusta non est lex, taken carefully, is still a fairly direct claim about the conditions a human law must meet to be genuine law. Finnis reframes the question again, using the idea of a focal (or central) meaning.

Finnis argues that 'law' and 'legal system' are used with a focal meaning — the central case is a legal system that genuinely serves the common good through practical reasonableness, using authority, coercion and determinatio for their proper purpose — and a range of peripheral cases, which share enough of the central case's features (institutions, procedures, claims to authority) to be called 'law' too, even though they fall short of serving the common good as fully, or at all. On this account, a seriously unjust legal system doesn't simply fail to be law; it is law, but only in a watered-down, peripheral sense — much as a corrupt friendship is still recognisably called a 'friendship', while falling well short of what friendship, at its best, actually is.

This softens the binary feel of lex injusta non est lex without abandoning natural law's core claim: legal validity, for Finnis, still answers to the theory's substantive moral commitments, but through a more flexible, graded picture of what 'counts as' law at all — one more resilient to Hart's coming objection that natural law simply can't accommodate the plain fact that unjust legal systems still function, are still obeyed, and are still recognisably legal systems by any ordinary use of the word.

components.definition: Finnis's device for classifying legal systems: the central (focal) case of 'law' is a system that genuinely serves the common good through practical reasonableness; peripheral cases share enough institutional features to be called law too, while falling short — sometimes far short — of the focal case.

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that Finnis's 'focal meaning' device gives exactly the same answer as Aquinas's lex injusta non est lex when applied to a seriously unjust legal system?
sliderLabels: Confident — the same answer, just relabelled
Confident — a genuinely different, more graded answer
interaction.correctPosition: Confident — a genuinely different, more graded answer
interaction.explanation: Finnis's move is more graded than a binary 'law or not law' test. A seriously unjust system is, for Finnis, still law — just a peripheral instance of it, falling well short of the focal case — rather than something whose status as law is directly denied, as Aquinas's stronger formulations can be read to suggest.

testPool.prompt: What does Finnis put at the centre of his revival of natural law, in place of Aquinas's theological scaffold?
acceptableAnswers: practical reason and the self-evident basic goods
testPool.modelAnswer: Practical reasonableness — an account of basic, self-evident forms of human flourishing and the requirements of reasonableness that structure how they should be pursued, developed without relying on theology.

acceptableAnswers: life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability/friendship, practical reasonableness, religion
testPool.modelAnswer: Life, knowledge, play, aesthetic experience, sociability (friendship), practical reasonableness, and religion (broadly understood).

testPool.prompt: Does Finnis rank his seven basic goods in order of importance?
options: No — he treats them as unranked and irreducible to one another
Yes — life is always ranked above the other six

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of Finnis's seven basic goods?
options: Knowledge
Sociability (friendship)
Wealth
Play
testPool.trapExplanation: Wealth doesn't appear on Finnis's list at all — it's an instrumental good, valuable as a means to other ends, not one of the seven basic, self-evidently worthwhile ends he identifies.

testPool.prompt: A student writes: 'Finnis derives the basic goods from facts about human biology, and is therefore vulnerable to the naturalistic fallacy in exactly the way he claims to avoid.' What is the most accurate response to this claim?
options: It correctly states Finnis's position and the objection succeeds without further argument
It misstates Finnis's position — he claims the basic goods are self-evident to practical reason, not derived from biological facts — so any critique has to engage with the self-evidence claim itself
Finnis has no answer to the naturalistic fallacy at all and simply ignores the objection
testPool.trapExplanation: The tempting error is treating Finnis as conceding a fact-to-value inference he explicitly denies making. He does have an answer — the self-evidence thesis — and a fair critique must engage with whether that thesis really escapes the objection, not attribute to him a move he disclaims.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states Finnis's self-evidence claim about the basic goods.
testPool.passage: Finnis does not attempt to derive the basic goods from prior premises about human nature through a chain of syllogistic reasoning. Instead, he holds that a good such as knowledge is grasped as self-evidently worthwhile by practical understanding, once one reflects on one's own engagement with inquiry. Critics dispute whether this successfully avoids the naturalistic fallacy, but it is, at minimum, a different kind of claim from a derivation.
testPool.ratioSentence: Instead, he holds that a good such as knowledge is grasped as self-evidently worthwhile by practical understanding, once one reflects on one's own engagement with inquiry.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that best explains why a determinatio is not a strict logical deduction from natural law.
testPool.passage: Natural law requires, in the abstract, that traffic move in a coordinated and predictable way, since coordination serves the basic good of life. It does not, however, specify which side of the road that coordination should occur on — either side would serve the underlying good equally well. A lawmaker's choice of one side over the other settles a question natural law itself leaves genuinely open, which is precisely why the choice is called a determinatio rather than a deduction.
testPool.ratioSentence: A lawmaker's choice of one side over the other settles a question natural law itself leaves genuinely open, which is precisely why the choice is called a determinatio rather than a deduction.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows the rule is best explained as a determinatio, rather than as directly required by natural law.
testPool.scenarioText: A local authority sets a maximum noise level for late-night construction work. Several different decibel thresholds would have adequately protected residents' rest, and the authority's chosen figure was one reasonable option among several rather than the only one available.
tappableSpans: several different decibel thresholds would have adequately protected residents' rest
testPool.correctSpan: several different decibel thresholds would have adequately protected residents' rest
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right. The presence of several equally reasonable options is the signature of a determinatio — natural law requires protecting rest in the abstract, but leaves the exact figure open, and the authority's choice is what makes one specific figure binding.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact showing more than one option would have worked equally well. That range of reasonable options is what marks a rule out as a determinatio rather than something natural law directly dictates.

testPool.prompt: Order the steps in Finnis's reasoning from a basic good to a binding positive-law rule.
items: Identify a basic good that practical reasonableness requires be served (e.g. life, through road safety)
Recognise that natural law leaves open several reasonable ways of serving that good (e.g. which side of the road)
A properly authorised lawmaker makes a reasonable choice among those open options (a determinatio)
The chosen rule becomes genuinely binding, even though the alternative option would have served the good equally well

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is best explained using Finnis's idea of 'focal meaning', rather than a simple binary 'is it law or not' test?
testPool.scenarioA: A legal scholar describes a legal system built on systematic racial oppression as 'law', while also saying it falls far short of what a legal system, at its best, is meant to be
testPool.scenarioB: A first-year student insists that any system enforced by courts and police must automatically count as a fully just legal order
testPool.explanation: A illustrates focal meaning precisely: the unjust system is still called 'law' — a peripheral instance — while being measured against, and falling short of, the focal case of a system that genuinely serves the common good. B collapses the distinction entirely and isn't using Finnis's framework at all.

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, which phrase signals that Finnis's account of legal validity is graded rather than binary?
options: 'a range of peripheral cases, which share enough of the central case's features to be called law too'
'the central case is a legal system that genuinely serves the common good'
'using authority, coercion and determinatio for their proper purpose'
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. The language of 'peripheral cases' that still count as law, alongside a 'central case', is what introduces gradation into Finnis's account — a system can be law in a weaker, peripheral sense without meeting the full focal-case standard.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The other two phrases describe the focal case itself. The phrase that introduces gradation is the one naming a further category — 'peripheral cases' — that still counts as law despite falling short of the central case.

testPool.prompt: A national parliament sets the voting age at 18. No natural-law principle dictates that precise number over, say, 17 or 19, but the general requirement of practical reasonableness supports having some settled, coordinated age of political participation. How should this rule be classified under Finnis's framework?
options: A determinatio — a reasonable specification of an open question, made binding by proper authority
A direct deduction from natural law, since only 18 could possibly be correct
Outside natural law altogether, because it involves a number rather than a moral principle
testPool.explanation: This is a textbook determinatio: practical reasonableness supports having a settled voting age (serving coordination and the good of participation), but leaves the specific figure open among several reasonable choices. The legislature's selection of 18 is what turns an open requirement into a binding, specific rule.

testPool.prompt: A regime enacts a statute requiring the summary execution of political dissidents, with courts and police fully enforcing it. Using Finnis's focal-meaning framework rather than a strict lex injusta non est lex test, which conclusion follows most precisely?
options: The statute is not law in any sense, and the question is closed
The statute is law only in a peripheral sense — it shares institutional features with the focal case of law but falls drastically short of serving the common good through practical reasonableness
The statute is a full focal-case instance of law because it is enforced by courts and police
testPool.explanation: Finnis's device allows the statute to be called 'law' — it has courts, police and the institutional trappings of a legal system — while still judging it a severely deficient, peripheral instance, since it fails almost entirely to serve the common good through practical reasonableness. That graded verdict is exactly what focal meaning is built to deliver, in contrast to a flatter binary test.

testPool.prompt: A city council debates two rival bylaws for regulating e-scooter speeds in pedestrian zones: an 8mph limit and a 6mph limit. Both figures are supported by broadly similar safety evidence, and reasonable experts disagree about which is preferable. The council adopts the 6mph limit. Analyse, using Finnis's framework, why the 6mph limit becomes binding even though 8mph would also have been a reasonable choice.
factsToOrder: Practical reasonableness requires some coordinated, predictable rule to protect pedestrians (the basic good of life)
Two different figures are both reasonably supported by the evidence
The council, as a properly authorised body, adopts one of the two reasonable figures
The chosen figure becomes a specific, binding rule

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule given; student applies it to the facts and writes the conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full analysis unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Why the council's chosen 6mph limit is binding, given that the rival 8mph limit would also have been a reasonable choice.
modelAnswer.rule: A determinatio is a reasonable choice, made by a properly authorised lawmaker, that settles one of several options natural law leaves genuinely open in order to serve a good natural law requires only in the abstract; it is binding not because it was the only reasonable option, but because a proper authority made a reasonable choice among genuinely open options.
modelAnswer.application: Practical reasonableness requires some coordinated speed rule to protect pedestrians, but does not itself dictate 6mph over 8mph — both are reasonably supported. The council's adoption of 6mph is therefore a determinatio: a reasonable specification, by a body with standing to make it, of an open question. The fact that 8mph would also have worked does not undermine 6mph's binding force, because determinatio does not require the chosen option to be the uniquely correct one, only a reasonable one properly settled by authority.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The 6mph limit binds because it is a valid determinatio — a reasonable choice by a proper authority among genuinely open options serving a basic good — not because it is the only figure natural law could have supported.

testPool.prompt: Does Finnis claim that his theory of the basic goods depends on, or is an argument for, theism?
options: No — he presents the basic goods and practical reasonableness as standing independently of theism
Yes — the entire theory collapses without a prior commitment to God

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The single most common mistake in this lesson's test items is attributing to Finnis a derivation of the basic goods from facts about human nature, which is precisely the naturalistic-fallacy move he explicitly disclaims. The second most common mistake is treating determinatio as a strict logical deduction, when its whole point is that natural law leaves the specific choice genuinely open until an authorised lawmaker settles it.
